blocks.text:
A SCHEMA FOR

1. The material signifiers

The first stage of the analytical process involves noting as much detail as possible about the chosen performance. At this stage I try to refrain from detailing the meanings that I have perceived m my viewing of the performance and concentrate on describing the material signifiers that carry the meanings I perceived. I begin by sketching the set (if visible before the performance begins) and the arrangement of stage and auditorium as I have found that this is a great aide-mémoire later.

I note as much detail as possible about the following categones and, while I have never found it possible or desirable to take notes during a performance, I do spend the interval(s) writing notes and then write extensive notes immediately after the performance while the memory is still fresh. It is a very striking aspect of the theatrical experience that the details become blurred in a relatively short time.

a) Stage-auditorium relationship

Size, distance, relative position;

Type of stage (e.g. proscenium/thrust/arena)

Set: visible/hidden (by what means) before action begins

Utilisation (if any) by actors of audience space

b) Decor/Objects

Detailed description of component elements of set (sketch, particular importance of exit points)

What changes take place and when?

Common features throughout?

Lighting

major changes

what purpose is served, what is underlying system?

Objects -make list

realistic! stylised/ transformable

associated with which characters/situations

referential connections (external coding)

c) Actors -physical features of performance

Costume, hair, make-up, masks, vocal quality

What changes are made during the action, and when?

Links/ contrasts between characters which are thus created

d) Utilisation of the scenic space by the actors

Relationship between "on" and "off" stage

how many "off" places are there?

function of doors and windows

are the "off" places positively or negatively valued?

Physical action/blocking

number of performers using scenic space

significant gesture and movement

significant juxtaposition of actor/actor, actor/object, and

actor/element of decor

e) Music and sound effects

what music is used, when is it introduced?

what sounds are used, when are they introduced?

The next three stages of the analysis occur in the days following the experience of the performance and they involve intensive reflection on the meanings created by the material signifiers that have been noted.

THE ANALYSIS OF PERFORMANCE

II. Narrative content/Performance segmentation

Stage two concerns both the narrative content and the way the performance was segmented, and frequently find that I need to write up my notes on this before I can go very far with my reflections on the connotational levels of the performance signs, or with the performance paradigms. I note the following:

What story is presented or what is the sequence of actions/events?

How many episodes? How are they signalled?

Are there different kinds of performativity involved in different episodes (e.g. are some enacted and others narrated)?

How is the stage action segmented?

number, nature, order, content of segments

is the segmentation clearly signalled?

means used (e.g. shifts in actorial presence, lighting, curtain, shifts in decor, etc.)

The important things to emerge here are the relationship between the performance segmentation and the narrative, the way the performance structures the narrative, and the implications that can be drawn from this structure.

blocks.text:
II. The paradigmatic axis

Max Frisch defined theatricality as "the magnetic field which exists between perception and imagination", and this idea is central to the spectator's experience of constructing meaning recreated here. The process involves considering all the details I listed in relation to the categories (a) to (e) in stage one, thinking about the meanings they conveyed, and the connotational levels I perceived then (or perceive now).

At this stage I look at the signs within each of the categories, and consider the system that seems to underpin the choices that have been made. More importantly, however, I begin to note the signs which seem to relate across the categories to form clusters of special significance. These clusters can be called performance paradigms. The data that has been collected and listed in stage one will be spaced out along the diachronic axis of the performance, but in order to make sense of it all it is necessary to find the significant repetitions, redundancies, contrasts, etc. which constitute the synchronic axis. Establishing the major performance paradigms enables me to articulate the meanings that this particular performance/ production created for me.

This is also the moment to consider the relationship between the performance paradigms and the narrative and/or ideas retained from the dialogue. It is only after doing all this that I feel ready to comment on the way the production in question has realised the fictional material it presents, and this leads me to the final stage of the analysis.

IV. Global statement

Here I draw on my findings in stages two and three and try to establish what I think the play/ performance is saying. In referring here to "play/performance" rather than some singular entity, I am acknowledging that there may be a disjunction between the ostensible content of the play/narrative and what the performance paradigms reveal (e.g. a politically progressive meaning undercut by aspects of its realisation, or something that is valorised in the dialogue and diegesis, being devalorised through other performance signs). I have noticed, from many years of using this schema and other questionnaires with students, that this question is something that theatregoers are often reluctant to tackle and yet it goes to the heart of the social function of theatre in our community.

This schema is posited on a number of assumptions that should be made clear at the outset. It is designed to deal with cultural performance, i.e. performances organised with aesthetic intent, rather than direct performance such as, for example, question time in Federal Parliament. While it can be adapted for a range of performance practices, it is most obviously applicable to theatrical performance, both traditional and avant-garde. It concentrates on the performance itself, rather than the spectator's horizon of expectation, or the way the performance was received by others in the community. These are important factors and they need to be taken into account insofar as they impact upon the spectator/analyst (Ubersfeld's questionnaire in Approaching Theatre is a useful means of establishing the context of reception for the analysis). My approach to performance analysis is also posited on the notion that spectators m the theatre do, by and large, try to make sense of what they see/hear. It is evident that in much postmodern work meanings may be glimpsed only in fragmentary moments, as is demonstrated m the perceptive writing about such performance that Keith Gallasch and Virginia Baxter regularly publish in the increasingly indispensable Rea/Time, but I think that even in this kind of work, the spectator is attempting to make connections and perceive structure. This is the trajectory that I trace in the schema which I include here, not because I think it is the only way to do analysis, but as a contribution to discussion about appropriate methodologies and to raise awareness of the critical choices that are necessarily and unavoidably involved in this complex task.

The analytical process, as I see it, involves four stages and it is my contention that they are cumulative and need to build on each other. While the precise order in which stages two and three are undertaken may vary, depending to a large extent on the nature of the performance, it seems to me that the analysis should begin with the description of the material signifiers of the performance (stage one) and end with a global statement about the meanings the analyst has constructed from it (stage four). It is evident that the spectator in the theatre does not separate the experience of the material reality of the performance from making sense of it, and as Martin and Sauter point out, the spectators' process involves a continual to-ing and fro-ing, "correcting from part to whole" (Martin & Sauter, 1995, 76- 77), as they attempt to make sense of what they see. However, for the purposes of analysis, it seems to me that it is helpful to create an artificial separation, and to hold off from the attribution of meaning until later in the analysis. It is, of course, true that when the analyst begins work on the analysis, he/she has already experienced the whole performance (possibly more than once), and has already been through the normal spectatorial process of making sense, of attributing meanings and perceiving connections, etc. This is doubtless why Patrice Pavis begins his questionnaire with a question about the overall experience of the performance.

A major reason for deferring until later in the analytical process statements about meaning, is that it obliges one to take into account a greater range of performance signs, countering the "sampling" that I have already said seems to me to constitute the normal spectator's mode of apprehension of performance, and the short circuit that occurs when spectators are so sure of the meanings they are perceiving that they fail to notice any elements that could undermine them. While I have established five major categories of performance sign that need to be taken into account, other theorists have sliced the cake differently, and it can certainly be argued that my perception of the dominant theatrical signifiers privileges a certain kind of performance. It is indeed my perception that space, activated and energised by the performer, is central to the communication that occurs in live performance, but whether or not this is accepted, all theorists would probably agree that the main task at the outset is to examine the material signifiers of the performance. If this stage of the work is undertaken as a group project, the subsequent pooling of observations and details reveals interesting differences between spectators in what they have noticed and what they remember.

The second stage, I suggest, is to consider the narrative content of the performance. This is a fairly vexed question, not so much because some performance genres have problematised the notion of fiction and even of narrative, as that it involves a different order of experience from the materiality of the performance. The stage m the analysis at which consideration of the narrative is introduced varies considerably: for Pavis, this is question 9 in his 14 part questionnaire, for Ubersfeld it is the final stage in the process, when the analyst considers the production as a whole, drawing out the significance of what it has done to the original material (whether this was a playtext, a body of myth or stories, or an idea or theme). I put the narrative structure together with segmentation of the performance continuum, firstly because in the text/character/narrative-based theatre of our mainstream tradition, the narrative is the most obvious means whereby the spectator perceives the segmentation (this happened, then this, then this), and secondly because the one is constructing and shaping the other. The point at this stage is to consider the way the narrative content has been shaped dramaturgically and, more importantly, how the performance signifiers construct, situate and comment on this. A play text may appear to contain a certain narrative, but the production of this in one mise en scene can differ so radically from another that it can legitimately be asked whether they have told the same story, and this of course is the major discovery of "directors5 theatre55 with its emphasis on working with classic texts, which are constantly remade and radically rethought through performance.

When analysing physical or non-text-based theatre, I would reverse the order of the two questions m this section, and examine first the segmentation of the performance and how this is signalled and then explore the narrative content, however fragmented and fragmentary, I found in the performance. The point, however, is still to examine the relation between the two, how the one is constructed by the other, and then to look at the way the dominant performance paradigms are shaping and commenting on the narrative.

Ml the theorists seem to recognise that the process of meaning making involves grouping the signs into meaningful clusters of some sort, but the terminology varies considerably here. Martin and Sauter have introduced the notion of the "dominant55 to address the way the spectator deals with the proliferation of signifiers, Anne Ubersfeld talks of "signifying ensembles55 and Pavis has developed the idea of "vectors55 (Martin & Sauter, 1995; Ubersfeld, 1981; Pavis, 1996), but all seem to me to be attempts to theorise something very similar. I have used the term "performance paradigm55 and this represents for me the third, and probably the most important, stage in the analytical process. The analyst, in describing the material signifiers of the performance, has already perceived denotative and connotative levels of meaning, but here the task is to move from the diachronic to the synchronic, to note the significant repetitions, redundancies, contrasts, etc. and to look for the jstem that seems to underpin the choices that have been made. The performance paradigms emerge from this sense of the system within the particular sign categories as well as from connections between the different sign systems.

For example, in Barry Kosky's production of Tartuffe for the Sydney Theatre Company, the dominant paradigm for me arose from the strong horizontal division of the stage space, the frenetic energy of the performers, repeatedly racing across the width of this two tiered space, the bold, primary colours of costumes and set, and the bright light. All this combined to create the idea of a puppet stage and the characters as puppets. The appearance of the King's emissary as marionnette, while countering the horizontal with a strong vertical (he descended on a harness from the flies, like any good deus ex machina) , reinforced the idea of the characters as mechanically motivated abstractions. The production was theatrically brilliant but afterwards I found myself wondering why I felt dissatisfied. It seems to me now that the answer is to be found in this dominant paradigm. The fact that all the characters, young and old, wise and foolish alike, became puppets meant that Ko sky lost some of the moral dimension of Moliereis play, and despite the energy and inventiveness of the production, it ended up permitting the spectators to avoid dealing with the relevance to contemporary Sydney society of Moliereis critique of hypocrisy.

The final stage is concerned with elaborating what the analyst considers the performance to be saying and it is my opinion that it is preferable to work through the detail of the material signifiers, the connotational levels of meaning the way these form clusters of special significance or paradigms, and to hold back from attributing meaning until one has worked systematically through the process. It is interesting to note that the meanings one thought were being conveyed, the meanings one took away from the first performance, are often considerably modified by the analytical process and the way it has obliged one to look again and again at certain elements. Sometimes the meaning I originally perceived is deepened and enriched by the analysis, sometimes I find quite different meanings, and sometimes I find that ostensible meanings have been subverted in some way by other factors. For example, the positive valorisation of family and home undercut by a stagng that, at a crucial moment, locates family space and forces threatening family through the same exit point.

There is no single way to do performance analysis, and indeed the nature of the performances impact upon the analytical method. Appropriate procedures for analysing text/character/narrative-based theatre may not work for physical performance or ritual or direct performance as the factors to be taken into account will be different. It is nevertheless my view that some version of my four point structure will be helpful: establish the material signifiers, note the sequence of events they present, extrapolate from this the dominant recurring paradigms or signifying ensembles, and then think about the overall significance to be deduced from the relation between the performance paradigms and the events or actions presented.

Acknowledging that performance analysis is not simply an extension of normal spectatorly practice, raises a number of questions about the type of access to performance that is necessary or desirable, and the extent to which one tries to emulate normal practice. Patrice Pavis claims that his questionnaire is designed to be used after one viewing of the performance and his remark about analysts who cheat (already mentioned above), takes this even further. In my view, it is entirely appropriate for the analyst to return over and over again to the performance, just as the literary critic reads the novel over and over, and the film analyst may view the film on an analector projector, and indeed, I would say that the level of complexity that can be reached after a single viewing is hardly doing justice to the creative efforts of the many people who have worked for weeks to construct the performance.

The key point is surely that the analyst should make clear at the outset whether the analysis is based on a single viewing by one person, on multiple viewings, on a single viewing by a group who have pooled their recollections, on insider knowledge of the performance derived from attendance at rehearsals, on use of sound or video recordings, or on any combination of these. All can be useful, all are methodologically justifiable, although the use of video poses problems in that the overlay of televisual information may distort the analysis, but the reader of the analysis needs to know the basis on which it was done.

Another general point concerns the stage of the performance experience at which the verbalising process begins. Actors and other spectators get anxious if people in the auditorium are taking notes, and indeed it can be seen as a subversion of the performance experience. More important is the problem of "fixing" the response too soon, and I have already mentioned the fact that people seem to need some critical distance before they are prepared to venture analytical commentary beyond immediately observable detail. The value of verbalising one's response is mentioned by Pavis and his questionnaire is designed to encourage this.1 In my experience, unless there is some attempt at verbalisation, preferably in writing, the performance begins very rapidly to recede from the memory. Verbalising clarifies the performance experience and can reveal things that one was not consciously aware of during the actual experience. Furthermore, it is only when the analysis is written up that there is some record that can serve the documentation purposes I see as one of the important functions of performance analysis.

The attempt to systematise the analytical process that is exemplified in my schema raises a number of problematical issues that have not really been solved in any of the models proposed by other theorists. The first involves the gap between listing observable details on the diachronic axis and "making sense", that is to say perceiving the system that is in operation and relating it to the referential context. While this is relatively easy within a given sign category such as costume or decor, it is much more complex across the sign categories. While I know from experience that the crucial step lies in constructing the performance paradigms, there is no formula for doing this. On some occasions the perception of paradigms is almost instantaneous with the perception of the signs themselves and seems to be part of the rapid semiotic processing of which the human mind is capable, but on others they emerge only much later in the analytical process and one has to make a conscious effort to extract them from the mass of detail.

The segmentation of the performance also raises problems, both in terms of the basis on which it is done and the stage at which it is brought into the analysis. It has been included in my proposed schema in a preliminary way in question Id): taking the utilisation of the performance space by the performers as one of the key material signtfiers, I suggest that entrances, exits and major movements within the scenic space be noted. The question of segmentation is then posed more explicitly in stage two, where it is seen in relation to the narrative content. It is, however, the movements of the performers into, out of and within the scenic space that is the major means of segmenting the performance continuum and of signalling this segmentation to the spectators. The difficulty here is that the one-time spectator tends to recall relatively little of the blocking and, unless there is a narrative to assist in remembering the sequence of events/actions, may also have only a ha2y recollection of the segmentation. Yet actors spend a substantial amount of rehearsal time on the blocking which constructs the basic sequence of events and articulates this in relation to the space, and a performance analysis based on the sort of intimate knowledge that comes from observing rehearsals reveals just how much meaning is being conveyed through the blocking and the segmentation that it signals2. This must be operative in the spectators' experience of the production but the fact that they cannot reconstruct it with any accuracy certainly creates a problem. The disjunction between the lack of detail in the average spectator's memory of the performance and the importance such detail assumes in an analysis based on recording or rehearsal observation where it is retrievable can perhaps be seen as more evidence of the distinction between the cognitive processes of spectators in the theatre and the task of performance analysis.

The related question of story or narrative content poses problems in terms of its location in the analysis. The task is to consider both the material signtfiers of the performance and the story or stories they tell, and to explore how the mode of telling, the choice of detail within each sign system and across the systems, functions to create and comment on these stories. While the spectator in the theatre is in fact experiencing the two simultaneously, the analyst has to separate them for the purposes of analytical clarity but the question of which comes first needs to be addressed. Ubersfeld says that when she is analysing a play text she begins by reconstructing the story, but when she is analysing a performance she begins with the physicality of the performance (Ubersfeld, 1991, 135-36). In my schema I suggest beginning with the matenal sigmfiers, partly because that relates more closely to the spectator's experience in the theatre (you go into the theatre, you look at the set, you see the actors coming on, you notice their appearance etc. before you have enough elements with which to construct a story), and partly because it is easier to notate the material details without worrying too much about meaning at that early stage. It is, however, an artificial separation and it functions to ensure that the analysis is based on as detailed an account of the material sigmfiers as possible.

Performance analysis, as I see it, imposes a discipline that normal spectatorial practice does not, and it aspires to a more complete accounting for the observed performance signs than the one-time spectator deems necessary, but it does not for all that lay claims to objectivity or to establishing definitive meanings. Meaning is created in a dynamic process by the spectator in his/her experience of the performance, and the meanings any spectator takes away from a performance are always partial, always shifting, ready to be modified in light of later experiences, other people's perceptions, etc. The analyst's experience is, m this respect, no different from the spectator's but the analyst has the added responsibility of making clear the process whereby the meanings have been reached. Setting out the stages of the analysis, as I have done here, and emphasising the processual nature of the analytical task makes it appropriate for me to end with Brecht's wonderful point about the actor in performance, for it holds equally true for the spectator and for the analysis of performance: "this is not magic, but work, my friends" (Brecht, 1976, 425).

{"path": "README.md", "markdown": "# Performance Analysis Schema Mapping Tool

A web-based tool that helps university students map, organise, and interpret the elements of a live performance using Gay McAuley's performance analysis schema — so they can write stronger, evidence-grounded analyses.

## The Problem

Performance analysis requires students to track many simultaneous elements across time — space, light, sound, movement, costume — and then identify the interpretive patterns (paradigms) that connect them. Without a structured tool, this process is overwhelmed by memory decay, sampling bias, and the difficulty of moving from raw observation to meaningful argument.

## The Vision

A two-stage digital tool that:
1. Gives students a **multi-track timeline** (like a DAW) to map observations across McAuley's five performance element categories as the performance unfolds
2. Lets students **sort observations into paradigm clusters** — the synchronic patterns that underpin their interpretive argument

The finished map is shareable, exportable, and serves as a direct scaffold for the written analysis essay.

## Success Criteria

- A student can set up a map for a new performance in under 2 minutes
- Observations can be entered and positioned on a track without technical friction
- The paradigm sorting stage produces a clear visual grouping that a student can directly reference while writing
- A completed map can be exported as PDF/image or shared via link in one click
- The tool reflects the creative, expressive nature of the subject matter — it doesn't feel like a spreadsheet

## Out of Scope

- AI-generated analysis or essay drafts
- Video playback or timestamping synced to actual recordings
- Discussion forums or class collaboration features
- Mobile/tablet support (desktop/laptop web browser only, for now)
- Institutional LMS integration (e.g. Canvas, Moodle)
- User accounts, login, or authentication

## Target Users

### Primary — University Students
Undergraduate or postgraduate students enrolled in theatre, performance studies, dance, or music courses that require formal performance analysis. They have seen a live performance (theatre, dance, or music/opera) and need to document, organise, and interpret what they observed.

They are comfortable with digital tools but not necessarily with technical software. They need something that feels intuitive and doesn't get in the way of thinking.

### Secondary — Academics / Tutors
Course teachers who receive a shared map link from a student for review or feedback purposes. They are read-only users — they don't create maps themselves (at this stage). They may be the ones who introduce students to the tool as part of course materials.

## Core User Flows

### Flow 1 — Create a New Map (Stage 1: Material Signifiers)

1. Student arrives at the tool homepage
2. Clicks "New Map" — enters a performance title and optionally a date/venue
3. A multi-track canvas loads with default tracks based on McAuley's five categories:
   - **Stage / Space** (stage-auditorium relationship)
   - **Decor, Set & Lighting**
   - **Objects & Props**
   - **Actors — Appearance** (costume, hair, makeup, masks, vocal quality)
   - **Actors — Movement & Blocking** (utilisation of scenic space, gesture, juxtaposition)
   - **Music & Sound**
4. Student defines time markers along the horizontal axis (e.g. "Scene 1", "Act 2 opening", "Climax", or custom labels — no fixed format)
5. Student clicks into a track cell and types an observation (free text)
6. Student can add custom tracks (e.g. "Audience response", "Lighting subtext")
7. Student can hide tracks they don't need
8. Map is auto-saved and a unique share link is generated

### Flow 2 — Paradigm Sorting (Stage 2: Synchronic Analysis)

1. Student switches to "Paradigm View" from within their map
2. All observations from the map are displayed as individual cards
3. Student creates named paradigm groups (e.g. "Puppetry / mechanisation", "Horizontal vs vertical tension")
4. Student drags observations into paradigm groups
5. Paradigm view can be exported or shared alongside the map

### Flow 3 — Export & Share

1. From either view, student clicks "Export" — downloads as PDF or image
2. Student clicks "Share" — copies a unique read-only URL to send to their tutor

## Design Direction

The tool should feel **creative and expressive** — it's a tool for analysing art, and it should reflect that. Not cold, not corporate, not spreadsheet-like.

Inspiration: the visual language of arts programmes, theatre posters, music notation software. A dark or rich colour palette would suit the subject matter. Typography should feel considered — perhaps serif headings with clean sans-serif UI text.

The multi-track canvas (Stage 1) can lean into the DAW metaphor visually — horizontal tracks, clear time markers, a sense of performance unfolding left to right.

The paradigm sorting view (Stage 2) should feel more like an ideas board — cards, groupings, a sense of clustering and discovery.

No strong brand guidelines exist yet. Colour palette and logo are TBD.

- Theatre / drama (including text-based, devised, and avant-garde)
- Dance (ballet, contemporary, physical theatre)
- Music / opera

{"path": "features/paradigm-sorting.feature.md", "markdown": "# Paradigm Sorting

## Goal

Help students move from diachronic observation (what happened across time) to synchronic interpretation (what patterns and clusters of meaning emerge) — operationalising McAuley's Stage 3 (The Paradigmatic Axis) and bridging toward Stage 4 (Global Statement).

## The Concept

As McAuley writes: "the data that has been collected... will be spaced out along the diachronic axis of the performance, but in order to make sense of it all it is necessary to find the significant repetitions, redundancies, contrasts, etc. which constitute the synchronic axis."

Paradigm sorting is the moment a student stops describing and starts interpreting. They pull observations from across all tracks and time points, group them into named clusters, and those clusters become the evidence base for their analytical argument.

## Interface

- Accessed via a **"Paradigm View"** toggle/tab from within the map
- All observations from the map are displayed as **cards** (showing the observation text, its track label, and its time marker)
- Students create named **paradigm groups** — colour-coded containers (e.g. "Puppetry / mechanisation", "Horizontal vs vertical tension", "Absence and presence")
- Students **drag cards into groups**
- One observation can belong to **multiple paradigms** (many-to-many)
- Unassigned observations remain in a holding area until grouped or deliberately left out

## User Flow

1. Student opens their map and switches to Paradigm View
2. All observations appear as cards in an unassigned holding area
3. Student clicks "Add Paradigm Group" and gives it a name and colour
4. Student drags observation cards into one or more groups
5. Student can rename paradigm groups at any time
6. Student can remove a card from a group (it returns to unassigned)
7. Student can add notes to a paradigm group (a free text field describing the interpretive claim)
8. Paradigm view is included in export and share

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] All observations from the map appear as cards in the paradigm view
- [ ] Each card shows: observation text, track label, time marker label
- [ ] Student can create a named, colour-coded paradigm group
- [ ] Student can drag observation cards into paradigm groups
- [ ] One card can exist in multiple paradigm groups simultaneously
- [ ] Unassigned cards remain visible in a holding area
- [ ] Student can add a free text note to each paradigm group
- [ ] Student can rename or delete a paradigm group
- [ ] Paradigm view is included in export (PDF/image)
- [ ] Changes to paradigms are auto-saved

## Edge Cases

- A map with no observations should show an empty paradigm view with a prompt to return to Stage 1
- Deleting a paradigm group should return its cards to unassigned (not delete the underlying observations)
- If the underlying observation is edited in the map view, the card in paradigm view should reflect the update
- Very large numbers of observations (50+) should remain navigable — consider search or filter by track

## Connection to the Essay

The paradigm view is the bridge to writing. A student with three or four well-populated paradigm groups has, in effect, the sections of their essay already structured. The tool does not generate the essay — but the paradigm groups become their argument structure, and the observation cards within each group become their evidence.
"}
